content.title: About
content.content: Cherry cobbler is a classic American dessert made of a sweet cherry filling topped with a flaky biscuit‑like crust. The tartness of the cherries balances the buttery, slightly sweet dough that turns golden and crisp when baked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cobbler originated in the 19th‑century United States as a simple way to use seasonal berries.
A scoop of vanilla ice cream is a traditional accompaniment.
The topping can be a runny batter or a more solid biscuit dough, depending on the recipe.
Original recipes used whole‑wheat flour, but today many variations use whole‑grain or gluten‑free flours.
Cobbler is often baked in ceramic dishes, which retain heat and give the crust extra crunch.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cherries contain anthocyanins that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cherry provides vitamin C, supporting immune function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from the fruit aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low‑fat filling
items.content: Most of the calories come from the crust, while the fruit portion is relatively low in fat.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Flavonoids in cherries may help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional crusts contain wheat flour, which is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Recipes often call for a generous amount of sugar, increasing the dessert’s calorie load.

items.title: Acidity of cherries
items.content: Those with acid reflux may experience discomfort after eating cherry cobbler.

items.title: Undercooked dough
items.content: If the crust is not baked through, it can remain dense and harder to digest.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cobbler warm, typically with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream. It can be eaten straight from the baking dish or sliced into individual portions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore the crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Creamy Italian Dressing Light is a low‑fat dressing made from dairy bases and flavored with classic Italian herbs and spices. It works well on salads, as a marinade for fish or chicken, and adds a smooth, buttery taste without excess calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dressing contains a blend of basil, oregano, garlic and onion typical of Italian cuisine.
The light version usually has about 30 % less fat than the regular creamy dressing.
It is frequently used in restaurant diet menus where flavor balance and calorie control are important.
The formula may include yogurt or skim milk, boosting its protein content.
It retains its flavor profile in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes the dressing more suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Probiotic source (when yogurt is used)
items.content: Yogurt in the recipe can help support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Dairy ingredients provide calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and yogurt supply riboflavin (B2), which participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Herbs and spices
items.content: Basil and oregano have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains dairy, which may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Those allergic to casein or whey should avoid this dressing.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some formulations may have higher sodium; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain recipes include stabilizers and preservatives that might be undesirable for sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use the dressing to coat salads, marinate chicken, fish or vegetables, or as a dip for bread and veggie sticks. It can also be stirred into pasta for a creamier texture without adding many calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is typically good for 7‑10 days. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

roast-beef-sandwich-on-white-with-cheese.title: Roast beef sandwich on white, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A roast beef sandwich on white bread with cheese is a classic handheld meal featuring thinly sliced roasted beef (roast beef) placed between two slices of soft white bread, topped with melted or aged cheese that gently softens from the warmth of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Roast beef is traditionally made from high‑quality beef, cooked at low temperature to retain juiciness.
The roast beef sandwich became popular in the United Kingdom in the early 20th century and is often served with horseradish or mustard.
White bread used in this sandwich is usually lightly toasted to prevent sogginess from meat juices.
Cheese can be cheddar, Swiss, or Gouda, depending on personal preference.
The sandwich is frequently served as a “corner cut” triangle, making it easy to eat on the go.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Roast beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese contain B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of meat, cheese, and bread provides a quick source of energy for active days.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and beef can be high in saturated fats, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Both cheese and prepared roast beef are often salty; excess sodium may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to dairy proteins found in cheese.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Low‑quality or undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically served fresh, cut in half or into triangles. It can be enhanced with mustard, horseradish, lettuce, or pickles for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, separate the components: store meat and cheese apart, and keep the bread in a dry place to avoid sogginess.

soft-drink-fruit-flavored-caffeine-free.title: Soft drink, fruit flavored, caffeine free

content.title: About
content.content: A fruit‑flavored, caffeine‑free soft drink is a refreshing carbonated beverage with a bright fruit taste. It contains no caffeine, making it suitable for children and people avoiding stimulants. The drink typically includes water, sugar (or sugar substitutes), fruit flavorings, acids, and carbon dioxide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit soft drinks often use natural or artificial flavorings that mimic berries, citrus or tropical fruits.
The lack of caffeine makes them popular among those monitoring stimulant intake and in children's nutrition.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the liquid creates the characteristic “fizz” that enhances flavor perception.
In some countries these drinks are classified as “sweet carbonated beverages,” affecting taxation.
Traditional versions can be high in sugar, so diet variants with sweeteners are frequently released.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Carbonated water helps maintain the body’s fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Vitamin profile
items.content: Some fruit drinks are fortified with vitamin C and other antioxidants, which may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Caffeine‑free
items.content: The absence of caffeine makes the beverage safe for children, pregnant individuals, and caffeine‑sensitive people.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular versions can contain a lot of sugar, increasing the risk of tooth decay, weight gain, and blood‑glucose disturbances.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Diet versions often use sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose) that may cause individual adverse reactions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acids (citric, phosphoric) can contribute to dental enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Consume
content.content: Serve chilled as a standalone refresher or use in cocktails, desserts, and fruit salads. For children, choose sugar‑free options.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.
